title: What the City said: Council questions to the administration

panel.summary: The administration's panel came after the AI companies and before public testimony. It ran about 1 hour 11 minutes. Sarah Milstein read the opening statement for OTI and DCWP, then Council Members asked questions.

officials.name: Sarah Milstein
officials.title: Deputy Commissioner for Strategic Advisory Services, Office of Technology and Innovation (OTI). Oversees the Office of Algorithmic Accountability and NYC Cyber Command.

officials.name: CJ Dixon
officials.title: Deputy Commissioner, NYC Cyber Command (OTI), and the City's Chief Information Security Officer.

officials.name: Samuel Levine
officials.title: Commissioner, Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP).

officials.name: Benjamin Krakauer
officials.title: First Deputy Commissioner, NYC Emergency Management (NYCEM).

officials.name: Carlos Ortiz
officials.title: Chief of Staff and Deputy Commissioner for External Affairs, DCWP. Sworn in; we could not tell whether he spoke.

titles_note: Titles as introduced at the hearing.
positions: Int 161 (De La Rosa)
Adds workforce impact to yearly reporting on City algorithmic tools
Agrees the issue matters, but says the bill would add nothing beyond the larger Local Law 25 workforce study.
No AI model marketed, sold or deployed in NYC without third-party validation and a human shut-off
Neither OTI nor Cyber Command is the best choice to lead it. DCWP supports the intent and is unsure third-party validators exist yet.
City contractors report AI safety incidents, with public notice in 24 hours
Not all AI threats are cyberattacks, and the bill does not address that. Existing breach law applies. 24-hour public notice would compromise an investigation and is inconsistent with current law.
Cyber Command and NYCEM write an AI emergency response plan
Laws, policies and protocols for breaches already apply, whatever the actor. Happy to discuss how it already coordinates with NYCEM.
Anyone can file AI complaints with DCWP
DCWP strongly supports the intent; concerned about volume, cost and expertise.
Data security, privacy and access rules for chatbot companies
DCWP has concerns: the approach is sound, but enforcing its data security and privacy rules would need technical and investigative capacity outside DCWP's scope.
AI ads must disclose third-party validation; no false safety claims
DCWP supports the disclosure. Unsure third-party validators exist yet. False ads are already illegal under City law.

questions: Has the City met with OpenAI, Anthropic or other frontier AI companies about how they would coordinate in a serious AI incident?
Press reports say the City's AI director resigned. The office was due to be running in June; why isn't it?
The Speaker says OTI issued guidance instead of the rulemaking her law requires. When will rules come?
What stops City staff from putting confidential data into AI tools?
Is OTI measuring AI's effect on the City workforce?
How many people work at Cyber Command, and how many jobs are open?
Her Int 161 would make the workforce report yearly. What do you know now?
What protects City workers from being replaced by AI?
Where are City agencies on using AI internally?
Agencies report their own AI use. What tools will the new office have to check, including for NYPD?
How ready is the City for AI-driven cyberattacks?
Should a kill switch live in Cyber Command?
Should "AI control" be a cybersecurity specialty?
To DCWP: what AI misuse worries you most?
To DCWP: are you staffed for this? Would a private right of action help?
Will the new AI reporting be on time? How many staff, and at what stage?
To DCWP: how is Local Law 144 on AI hiring tools working?
Do you have someone for the director role?
Where is hiring for the six new positions, and what is slowing it?
How is the office protecting City workers as AI changes?
What is New York's AI "win"? Is OTI's AI guidance binding? Is there an approved tool list? How should buying AI work?
She says agencies are using ChatGPT, Claude and other tools. What is the policy? Do contracts protect constituent data?
Who is responsible for staff using tools that are not approved?
You said not all threats to AI systems are cyberattacks. What do you mean?
How does an agency start using a new AI model?
Does the City run models in its own data centers or on vendor clouds?
What do you do about an AI product that misbehaves?
How much does the City spend on outside AI consultants?
If an AI agent hacked a City system, is the City ready? Do AI companies have a contact for incidents?
Does an AI emergency plan already exist?
How does OTI keep HRA's automated screening tools from being biased against low-income New Yorkers?
To DCWP: what would you need to handle AI complaints?
What is the timeline for the Local Law 25 workforce study?

sections.who: Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers (read by the chair)
questions: What would an AI attack on emergency systems look like, and is there a plan? How does NYCEM keep its alerts trusted?
